learning_outcomes.description: Understand some of the central themes and concepts in Western political thought.
Appreciate the intellectual challenge of recovering what past authors meant by the things they wrote.
Recognise and understand the importance of conflict in the development of ideas, texts, and identities.
Understand the way disciplinary canons are formed and contested.
Be aware of the historical reception and re-interpretation of political ideas and ideals.
Be able to position key ideas and texts in relation to diverse civilisational groupings.
Appreciate the different ends of politics.
Understand the challenges and opportunities in applying their knowledge to studying contemporary political problems.
Demonstrate an ability to communicate their understanding of Western political thought through modes of written and oral expression appropriate to the discipline of politics.

assessments.task_description:
Video Presentation

Each student is required to make a video presentation (no more than 4 minutes) analysing the vision of politics conveyed in one of the following foundational texts:

  • Plato's Republic
  • Machiavelli's The Prince
  • Hobbes's Leviathan
  • Rousseau's The Social Contract and State of War


Your presentation must be anchored in a specific question, disagreement, or interpretive move that arose in your seminar's discussion of the text. This is not a framing device to be mentioned in passing; it is the starting point for your analysis. Begin by identifying a question or genuine point of contention from your seminar (a question that split opinion, an interpretive problem the group struggled with, a claim someone made that you want to test) and build your presentation as a response to it. You are not summarising the text in general; you are using the seminar's encounter with the text as the occasion for your own argument.

From that anchor, your presentation should develop an argument that engages the following dimensions:

  1. The Vision of Politics: What conception of politics is articulated in the text? Consider themes such as justice, power, sovereignty, inequality, nature, or law. What is politics for, and how should it be structured or conducted? To what end?
  2. The Author's Political Intentions: What is the main point or purpose of the text? What problem or concern is the author responding to? What kind of political change, reform, or understanding is the author seeking or legitimising? What audience(s) might they be trying to persuade?
  3. Genre and Style: How does the text's form or genre (e.g., dialogue, mirror-for-princes, treatise, essay) or rhetorical style (e.g., irony, persuasion, satire, exhortation) shape its political argument? Is the style part of the politics or in tension with it?

You do not need to address all three dimensions equally or exhaustively; let the seminar question you've chosen determine which of these matters most for your argument.

Expectations

  • Seminar anchoring: Open with, and build around, an identifiable question, disagreement, or interpretive moment from your seminar's discussion of the text. Generic references to ‘class discussion’ will not satisfy this requirement.
  • Textual grounding: Anchor your claims in specific passages or ideas from the text. Quote or paraphrase as needed.
  • Historical sensitivity: Situate the author in his or her historical and intellectual context.
  • Clarity and structure: Present a clear argument with a logical flow. Use visuals to assist and complement the argument.
  • Timing: The presentation should be no more than 4 minutes.


**Note on AI use: While UQ in its wisdom prevents me from prohibiting AI use in assessments, I strongly encourage you to approach AI tools thoughtfully and limit their role in the preparation and writing of your essay. On submission of your video presentation, your essay, and any other submissions for WCIV2700 you are required to fill out the course AI Declaration Coversheet.

**Information on making and uploading your video presentation: Students must upload a video version of this presentation. Instructions about filming a video and uploading it can be found on the UQ website (https://web.library.uq.edu.au/library-services/it/learnuq-blackboard-help/learnuq-assessment/blackboard-assignments).

Two software options available through UQ are Zoom and EchoVideo. If you are unfamiliar with these technologies, the Library has prepared useful guides. They are available here: 

https://web.library.uq.edu.au/library-services/it/learnuq-blackboard-help/learnuq-assessment/recording-video-assignments-zoom

https://web.library.uq.edu.au/library-services/it/learnuq-blackboard-help/learnuq-assessment/blackboard-assignments/submit-video-assignment-echovideo-original

assessments.task_description:
Task Description: This is a 10-minute individual oral examination designed to assess your understanding of course texts through spontaneous discussion.

Assessment Process: You will be scheduled for an individual meeting with the course coordinator.

  1. Text selection and reading: At the start of your oral assessment, you will nominate two texts (and passages from each text) from the course readings (excluding any text that is the focus of your research essay). The coordinator will select one of your nominated texts and ask you to read aloud a selected passage from your nominated text. Bring physical copies of both selected passages to your assessment (including page numbers in the prescribed course text. Students should not bring any other printed matter to the oral assessment (eg., a prepared print-out of the opening statement or other extended notes).
  2. Opening statement: The coordinator will then ask you to provide a brief exegesis and explanation of the chosen passage.
  3. Follow-up discussion: Follow-up questions will be asked to help you expand, clarify, or deepen your initial response. The coordinator will also pose further questions asking you to relate your selected passage and text to other texts studied in the course and to broader course-related themes and concepts.


All questions are designed to give you opportunities to demonstrate your knowledge—they are not intended to trick or intimidate you.

The session will be audio recorded for assessment purposes


Preparation:

  • Review all course texts thoroughly, focusing on key arguments, themes, and concepts.
  • Select two texts as the starting point of your oral assessment.
  • Choose a specific passage from each text that you consider significant for understanding politics or a specific political concept or argument.
  • Practice articulating your thoughts about texts clearly and concisely.
  • Bring physical copies of both selected passages to your assessment
  • Be prepared to discuss any text, including the one you wrote about in your research essay


Assessment Criteria:

Content (Knowledge & Analysis):

  • Completeness and accuracy of responses
  • Demonstration of close engagement with the text
  • Quality of analysis and interpretation
  • Understanding of connections between the text and course themes
  • Breadth and depth of knowledge displayed


Communication (Eloquence & Clarity):

  • Clear oral expression and organization of ideas
  • Effective use of relevant concepts, terminology, and examples
  • Ability to construct and articulate persuasive arguments
  • Overall coherence and engagement in scholarly discussion


Note: This assessment evaluates your ability to think and communicate spontaneously about course materials, demonstrating both your understanding of the texts and your capacity to engage in scholarly discussion about course-related themes and concepts.

learning_activities.topic:
Studying Western Visions of Politics

How and why should we study the history of (western) political thought? Which texts should we study, and why? How are canons formed, and by whom? And how do we engage with the texts that are selected? These questions immediately raise issues of method and purpose. We will consider two rival approaches: Quentin Skinner's contextual intellectual history, which seeks to recover what an author was doing in writing a text (‘seeing things their way’), and Sheldon Wolin's political theory, which conceives the theorist's task as building a vision of political life that claims some purchase beyond the moment of its composition (‘to transcend history’). Both approaches engage the past, but they disagree about the purpose of recovering a past text. What's at stake in this rivalry? Why do scholars talk about ‘visions of politics’ at all? And can these visions offer, as some have claimed, a form of solace or reconciliation in a disenchanted world, a question we will return to when we encounter twentieth century thinkers?


Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06, L07, L08, L09

Politics as Philosophy: Plato's Republic

Plato's Republic is a foundational text that established the western discourse of political philosophy. Why is The Republic structured as a dialogue? How does Plato present the figure of Socrates? How does Plato conceptualise justice and the good life? What role does philosophy play in the Platonic vision of politics? Why does Plato idealise the philosopher as ruler? What are the virtues required of a ruler? Why does Plato deprecate democracy and poetry?

learning_activities.topic:
The Autonomy of Politics: Machiavelli's The Prince

Machiavelli's The Prince is a classic political statement from the Italian Renaissance. Machiavelli's explosive little book built on humanist themes but scandalously rejected the notion that politics should be governed by moral-theological principles. To what extent did Machiavelli's diplomatic and political experience inform his vision of politics? What is the genre in which The Prince is written? What was his purpose? What are the virtues required of the prince? What happens to notions of justice and the good life in this vision of politics? How do virtu and Fortuna function in Machiavelli's vision of politics?


Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
Politics and the Paradoxes of Civil Bonds: Rousseau's Social Contract and the ‘State of War

The lecture will examine Rousseau's Social Contract and his essay on the ‘State of War’, contextualising the questions they address regarding legitimate political institutions and practices. The republican arguments of the self-styled ‘citizen of Geneva’ were crucial in influencing French revolutionaries and other proponents of popular sovereignty, for whom the state serves as a vehicle for the formation of a moral community; a community whose formation, Rousseau came to argue, does nothing to resolve, and may even intensify, the condition of war between states.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
Politics as Civil Science: Hobbes's Leviathan

The Leviathan is a monumental text of political theory written in the context of the English civil war. Hobbes's masterpiece defines and legitimises the notion of state sovereignty; a notion that has decisively shaped the modern world for better or worse. What were his intentions given the political and religious context of England and Europe? How does he construe the relationship between protection and obedience? How does Hobbes understand the office or role of sovereign? What are the virtues required of a sovereign? What function is served by Hobbes's myth of the state of nature, and what does that myth tell us about his vision of politics?


Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
Moralising International Politics: Kant's Perpetual Peace

The lecture will examine Immanuel Kant's essay on ‘Perpetual Peace’. It will situate the essay in Enlightenment themes and concepts, and explain Kant's normative critique of international politics; a critique framed, pointedly, in the form of a mock peace treaty responding to the diplomatic conventions of Kant's own day. The lecture will also consider Kant's essay as a response to the problem of international right that Rousseau had raised but left unresolved.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
Politics and the Paradoxes of Civil Bonds: Rousseau's Social Contract and the ‘State of War

Rousseau's Social Contract begins with a paradox: ‘man was born free, and everywhere he is in chains’. How does Rousseau seek to resolve this paradox? How does Rousseau's notion of the social contract differ from Hobbes's? What is the ‘general will’? How does the social contract transform individuals? What roles do the legislator and civil religion play in Rousseau's vision of politics? Finally, turning to his essay on the ‘State of War’, if the social contract solves the problem of legitimacy and moral community within the state, what happens to that problem between states? Why does Rousseau think the formation of political societies intensifies, rather than resolves, the condition of war among them, and what does this suggest about the limits of the vision of politics he constructs in the Social Contract?

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

Politics as Social Revolution: Marx & Engels' Communist Manifesto

The lecture will present the arguments of Marx and Engels' Communist Manifesto, one of the most influential texts of modern political thought. The critique of industrial capitalism and arguments to expand freedom and justice will be contextualised to understand the transformation of politics envisaged by Marx and Engels.

learning_activities.topic:
Moralising International Politics: Kant's Perpetual Peace

Kant's celebrated essay on ‘Perpetual Peace’ offers a transformative vision of international relations. Drawing on Enlightenment and Revolutionary ideals of universal freedom, justice, and rights, Kant devises a project for perpetual peace that aims to transform the system of independent sovereign states into a confederation of states governed by cosmopolitan law. Why does Kant cast his argument in the form of a peace treaty, complete with ‘preliminary’ and ‘definitive’ articles, and what is achieved by that choice of genre? How does Kant's proposal answer, or fail to answer, the problem Rousseau identified in the ‘State of War’, that the formation of political societies intensifies rather than resolves the condition of war between them? What is ‘cosmopolitan law’, and how does it differ from the law that governs relations between sovereign states? Finally, is Kant's project best understood as an act of vision-making extended to the international sphere itself, one which imagines not just a legitimate state, but a wholly transformed global system of states?

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
Politics as a Vocation: Max Weber

This lecture will situate Weber's famous lecture, 'Politics as a Vocation' in relation to his earlier, and equally famous and significant lecture on 'Science as a Vocation'. In these lectures, delivered to German university students in 1917 and 1919 respectively, Weber affirmed that different spheres of life should be seen as cultivating different values and responsibilities. The lecture will outline and explain Weber's conception of politics in a disenchanted world.

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
Politics as Social Revolution: Marx & Engels' Communist Manifesto

A powerful polemic about industrial capitalism's transformation of the modern world. We examine the Manifesto's critique of political economy and its analysis in terms of class struggle. How does Marx's conception of socialism shape notions of power, freedom, civil society, the state, etc? How do Marx and Engels' use of political concepts differ from previous European thinkers? What was the purpose of this text? How did it reshape German idealist philosophy? What, if anything, does Marx's transformative vision of politics hold in common with other thinkers we have studied in this course?

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

Politics as the Recovery of Lost Treasure: Arendt's On Revolution

The lecture will introduce students to the thinking of one of the twentieth century's most significant political theorists, Hannah Arendt. Her book On Revolution represents a critical engagement with one of the key concepts of western political thought, read here alongside the founding documents of the two revolutions she compares: the American Declaration of Independence and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen.

learning_activities.topic:
Politics as a Vocation: Max Weber

Weber's lecture on 'Politics as a Vocation' is rightly regarded as a major twentieth-century statement on what it means to engage in politics in the modern world. Yet it raised many controversies and questions. Why did Weber conceive of politics as a vocation? What does that imply? How should political actors conduct themselves? What are the markers of political leadership? What role does charisma play in politics? What is at stake in the distinction Weber makes between an ethic of conviction and an ethic of responsibility? Finally, is Weber's lecture best understood as a response to the specific crisis of authority in Germany in 1919, or as a vision of the political vocation as such, for any disenchanted age? And does Weber's ethic of responsibility offer solace in a disenchanted world, or does he deliberately deny us that comfort?

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
Shklar's Liberalism of Fear

This lecture will examine Judith Shklar's influential essay ‘The Liberalism of Fear’ as a distinctive contribution to late twentieth-century liberal political theory. It will situate Shklar's work within post-war liberalism and its critics — both the communitarian challenge to liberal theory and liberalism's own tendency toward comprehensive philosophical justification — and within the historical experience of political cruelty and oppression that shapes her argument. We will explore how Shklar's ‘liberalism of fear’ offers a minimalist yet robust defence of liberal institutions grounded not in grand philosophical theories or a positive vision of the good life, but in the basic human need for protection from cruelty and the abuse of power.

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09
learning_activities.topic_description: Shklar's Liberalism of Fear This lecture will examine Judith Shklar's influential essay ‘The Liberalism of Fear’ as a distinctive contribution to late twentieth-century liberal political theory. It will situate Shklar's work within post-war liberalism and its critics — both the communitarian challenge to liberal theory and liberalism's own tendency toward comprehensive philosophical justification — and within the historical experience of political cruelty and oppression that shapes her argument. We will explore how Shklar's ‘liberalism of fear’ offers a minimalist yet robust defence of liberal institutions grounded not in grand philosophical theories or a positive vision of the good life, but in the basic human need for protection from cruelty and the abuse of power.

learning_activities.topic:
Politics as the Recovery of Lost Treasure: Arendt's On Revolution

This penetrating and provocative book presents historically-informed theoretical reflections on one of the great modern political themes, and this week we read it alongside the two documents at its centre: the American Declaration of Independence and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen. How did Arendt frame her approach to the study of revolution? What role does she see for pity and compassion in politics? What is the place of violence in politics? What does Arendt mean by ‘the social question’, and how does she see its function in political life? What does Arendt see as the main differences between the American and French revolutions, and how far do the declarations themselves bear out that difference? Finally, what is the ‘lost treasure’ Arendt believes the revolutionary tradition buried, and can it still be recovered? What would that recovery mean for how we understand political freedom today?

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
Politics as Justice: Uluru Statement from the Heart

This lecture introduces students to a contemporary Australian classic of political thought, the Uluru Statement from the Heart. It will also examine Noel Pearson's essay ‘A Rightful Place’ as a leading Indigenous advocate's case for constitutional recognition, one that draws on the resources of western political thought — including its liberal and historical traditions — even as it insists on the irreducible place of Indigenous heritage in the Australian nation. It will then turn to the Uluru Statement itself, reflecting on the dialogue process that produced it and on its defining political concepts and themes, considering how the Statement builds on, and moves beyond, the case Pearson had made.

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
Shklar's Liberalism of Fear

Shklar's essay on ‘The Liberalism of Fear’ presents a provocative reimagining of liberal theory that prioritises the prevention of cruelty over the promotion of positive goods. What does Shklar mean when she argues that liberalism should be grounded in fear rather than hope? How does her approach differ from other liberal approaches that emphasise rights, autonomy, or justice? What are the implications of her claim that liberalism's primary virtue lies in ‘putting cruelty first’? How does her pessimistic realism challenge more optimistic visions of political life while still maintaining a commitment to liberal democratic institutions? Finally, is Shklar's liberalism of fear itself a vision of politics, or a deliberate refusal of vision-making? Is it perhaps an argument that the pursuit of grand visions is precisely what has licensed so much political cruelty, and that liberal theory should protect us from visions rather than offer one? 

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09

learning_activities.topic:
Politics as Justice: Uluru Statement from the Heart

We examine Noel Pearson's ‘A Rightful Place’ alongside the Referendum Council's Uluru Statement from the Heart, considering the Statement in the context of its production — dialogue among Indigenous communities and the colonial-settler state — and the way it draws on key western political concepts while introducing Indigenous themes through the concept of Makarrata. How does Pearson make the case for recognition, and what role do western political ideas play in his argument? What is the purpose of the Uluru Statement? What is it calling for? What is the genre of this text, and to whom is it addressed? Does it reflect a sense of crisis in western political thought? How does it relate to the other historic Declarations examined in this course? How do its conceptions of power, authority, and truth compare to those we have studied? Finally, to what extent does the Uluru Statement reflect, or reject, western visions of politics — and does Pearson's essay suggest that ‘reflecting’ and ‘rejecting’ a tradition of political thought can be the same act?

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L07, L08, L09
